extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and humor/human-behavior enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on writing jokes and understanding why jokes are funny, based on Greg Dean’s Step by Step Stand-Up Comedy; covers theory (why jokes work) and a practical prospecting system (Joke Map + Joke Mine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part joke structure: setup and punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: All jokes are made up of 2 parts — the setup and the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The setup creates expectations (a 1st Story) and the punchline provides the surprise (a 2nd Story). Note: "lots of jokes don’t have a spoken setup" because the setup can be implied. Example: Stephen King line analyzed as setup + punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor by surprise / expectation violation
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for something to be funny, it has to surprise you: the setup creates an expectation and the punchline surprises you with something different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dean: “The setup of a joke creates a 1st Story in our minds that leads us to expect something; then the punch surprises us with a 2nd Story that’s compatible with, yet somehow different from, what we’re expecting.” Example: Stephen King quote — the punchline forces re-interpretation. The momentary disorientation is where the humor lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility between the two stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline must present a 2nd Story that is compatible with, yet different from, the 1st Story the audience was following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second story should fit the established facts enough to be plausible but differ in key interpretation so surprise occurs. Compatibility prevents the punch from feeling random and preserves the link between setup and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied setup / world-knowledge setups
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes don’t need an explicit spoken setup because the audience's knowledge of the world supplies the initial story and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sight gags and physical comedy often rely on implied setup (e.g., expecting a dog to land on the couch). The audience automatically supplies assumptions based on prior experiences, cultural norms, and stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose topics that present something wrong / uncomfortable
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a topic that is a single subject presenting something wrong; humor evolved to cope with painful things, so uncomfortable topics often produce stronger jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topic should be broad enough to yield multiple jokes (e.g., a breakup, family, annoyances). The author: “your jokes will be better if you choose a topic that is uncomfortable for you or for others.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Map: generate association lists to create multiple setups
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a Joke Map to focus on a topic and write an association list (ideas, people, items) to generate a bunch of possible setups from that single topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example process: Topic = my family → association list (mother, father, vacations) → determine punch premises and reversed setups. The Map helps build a set by producing many setup options from one topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch premise and reversing to create setups
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a punch premise (a negative feeling or complaint) and reverse it to make the setup premise (the 1st Story) that you will then subvert with the punch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: punch premise = “My relationship with my mother was very bad.” Reverse to setup = “my relationship with my mother was very good.” Then invent setups consistent with that reversed premise to be subverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Mine: pick an assumption and its connector
rubrics_metrics.description: Drill down on a chosen setup by listing assumptions that audience makes and selecting the connector—the element (word/action) that causes the assumed interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connector is the thing that makes us believe the assumption (e.g., the word “call” in “I call my mom all the time”). Once connector is identified, search for alternative interpretations (reinterpretations) that create new story lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate reinterpretations / alternative readings
rubrics_metrics.description: For the connector/assumption, brainstorm alternative interpretations (reinterpretations) that could plausibly replace the audience’s assumed meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for “call”: telephone, call someone’s name, call a rude name, referee call. Dean notes choosing the most obvious reinterpretation sometimes helps because it’s what the audience will mentally reach for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal the twist at the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose the punchline so that the reveal (the reinterpretation) comes at the end, delivering the surprise after the audience has committed to the first story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author: “turn that story into an edited punchline — preferably with the reveal at the end.” Example joke: “I call my mother all the time, but in polite company, I can’t tell you what I call her!”

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a set by mining multiple punch premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple negative opinions/punch premises from your association list to create several related jokes and thereby build a set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have a bunch of negative opinions about a topic, write jokes about each of them — that's how you assemble a routine rather than isolated one-liners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use obvious reinterpretations when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes choosing the most obvious reinterpretation of a connector helps the joke because it matches what the audience will immediately think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increases the chance the audience follows the same mental path and is surprised by your chosen twist; it's a tactical choice rather than a fixed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/phonetic tips: hard consonants and quoting in character
rubrics_metrics.description: Small delivery and sound choices can affect funniness: hard consonants are funnier than soft ones, and quoting in character tends to be preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are ancillary tips from Dean: favor stronger consonant sounds for punch impact and perform quoted material in character to enhance comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice the skill of reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to see the typical interpretation and immediately think of alternate interpretations is part innate and part practice; it can be trained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author’s experience: using the system with family produced jokes with effort; practice and training make prospecting easier over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and diagrams to analyze and edit jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Break jokes into component parts (diagram) to show function and provide terminology for creation and editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dean’s Joke Diagram / Prospector System helps dissect classic jokes (Groucho Marx example) and supports systematic editing—use diagrams during writing to identify connectors, assumptions, and where to place the reveal.
